prompt.brief: Design a GPU cluster manager for ML training that schedules distributed jobs, allocates scarce accelerator and network resources across tenants, supports preemption and checkpoint recovery, and optimizes utilization and cost.
successSignals: Model job requirements, GPU type/count, topology, checkpoints, priority, quota, reservation, and tenant fairness explicitly.
Schedule gang jobs with topology awareness for NVLink/NVSwitch, detect unhealthy devices, and reclaim capacity safely.
Separate desired job state from node observations, utilization telemetry, billing, and checkpoint storage.
Explain preemption policy, starvation, elastic training, node loss, confidential data, quotas, and cost attribution.

functional: Submit training jobs, validate resource requests, queue by priority and fair share, allocate GPUs, and launch distributed workers.
Expose queue wait, placement, GPU health, utilization, preemption, checkpoint, restart, completion, and cost state.
Support tenant quotas, reservations, cancellation, checkpoint restore, chargeback, node drain, and administrative audit.
nonFunctional: Target above 80% aggregate GPU utilization without violating latency, fairness, or thermal and power limits.
Manage 10,000 GPUs and thousands of concurrent jobs with scheduler shards and per-tenant admission control.
Make allocation, preemption, checkpoint, and billing events idempotent; never allocate one GPU to two jobs.
Drain unhealthy nodes, restore from checkpoints, and preserve queued intent when scheduler or telemetry services fail.
scaleAssumptions: Operate 10,000 GPUs across accelerator generations, regions, and network topologies.
Partition scheduling by cluster, tenant, queue, and accelerator type; isolate large distributed jobs.
Retain job specifications, allocation decisions, device health, checkpoints, utilization samples, and billing evidence.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the GPU cluster manager commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional GPU cluster manager writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return GPU cluster manager version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition GPU cluster manager by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound GPU cluster manager work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for GPU cluster manager projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable GPU cluster manager projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable GPU cluster manager records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure GPU cluster manager latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.

rubric.description: The answer defines admission, fair-share scheduling, topology-aware placement, preemption, checkpoints, scale, and failure recovery.
Entities and keys cover tenants, jobs, queues, GPU nodes, leases, allocations, quotas, checkpoints, and scheduler epochs.
Partitioning, cache behavior, queues, backpressure, and hot-key handling are explicit.
Idempotency, replay, recovery, degraded reads, and observability protect committed state.
The candidate can explain GPU cluster manager consistency, push/pull, managed services, and the scale boundary.
